original_question.stem: A non-profit consumer organisation receives two requests. In case (i), one purchaser asks the organisation to lodge a consumer-court complaint on that purchaser’s behalf about a defective product. In case (ii), a residents’ group asks it to initiate a consumer-court case concerning an unfair seller practice affecting consumers generally; no individual is seeking the case on their behalf. Which pair correctly classifies the organisation’s role in (i) and (ii), respectively?
options: (i) Initiate a case in the general public interest; (ii) lodge a complaint on behalf of an individual consumer
(i) Provide legal assistance; (ii) initiate a case in the general public interest
(i) Lodge a complaint on behalf of an individual consumer; (ii) initiate a case in the general public interest
(i) Encourage consumers to protest; (ii) provide legal assistance

records.original_explanation: A consumer organisation may file a consumer-court complaint on behalf of an individual consumer. Separately, taking the initiative to file a case in a consumer court is identified as a role when the case is in the interest of the general public, not an individual. The two requests therefore match the roles in option C, respectively.

original_question.stem: A self-service fast-food chain uses a waiting-time standard for customers. After an internal business change, management finds that the existing standard is no longer realistic. What should management do?
options: Modify the standard so that it is realistic in the changed business environment.
Keep the standard unchanged once it has been set.
Modify the standard after every internal change, even when it remains realistic.
Treat a modified standard as no longer serving as a benchmark.

records.original_explanation: Standards are benchmarks and should be flexible enough to be modified when required. Since the internal change has made this standard unrealistic, management may modify it to make it realistic in the changed business environment.

reasons: failed:source_support
failed:source_support

The stem says the waiting-time standard is no longer realistic. The source states that standards should be flexible and modified when required to remain realistic in a changed business environment, supporting A.

original_question.stem: A firm’s plan sets a monthly production standard of 1,000 units for each of two units. At month-end, Unit P has produced 990 units and Unit Q has produced 800 units. Which approach should the manager use when determining corrective action?
options: Ignore the size of each shortfall and prescribe the same action solely because both units are below standard.
Treat the difference between the units’ actual outputs as each unit’s deviation, without comparing output with its own standard.
Compare each unit’s output with its own standard and let the extent of its deviation inform the nature of corrective action.
Use the actual outputs alone to determine corrective action, without referring to the planned standards.

records.original_explanation: Unit P is 10 units below its standard, while Unit Q is 200 units below its standard. Planning provides the basis of control, and the nature of corrective action depends on the extent of deviation from the standard. Therefore, each unit’s output should be compared with its own standard; the question does not specify the particular corrective actions.

The objective of the current year has also been clearly stated which is to increase capacity by 1500 ‑2000 more professionals. Since planning is the primary function of management they have set their objectives first. Thus, all businesses follow a set patter n of planning. You will be able to find some similarities in the features of planning and what you see in real life. Try and identify them. The planning function of the management has certain special features. These features throw light on its nature and scope. (i) Planning focuses on achieving objectives: Organisations are set up with a general purpose in view. Specific goals are set out in the plans along with the activities to be undertaken to achieve the goals. Thus, planning is purposeful. Planning has no meaning unless it contributes to the achievement of predetermined organisational goals. (ii) Planning is a primary function of management: Planning lays down the base for other functions of management. All other managerial functions are performed within the framework of the plans drawn. Thus, planning precedes other functions. This is also referred to as the primacy of planning. The various functions of management are interrelated and equally important. However, planning provides the basis of all other functions. (iii) Planning is pervasive: Planning is requir ed at all levels of management as well as in all departments of the organisation. It is not an exclusive function of top management nor of any particular department. But the scope of planning differs at different levels and among different departments. For example, the top management undertakes planning for the organisation as a whole. Middle management does the departmental planning. At the lowest level, day ‑to‑day operational planning is done by supervisors. (iv) Planning is continuous: Plans are prepar ed for a specific period of time, may be for a month, a quarter, or a year. At a small organisation, the line manager is reviewing two career moves: Employee P would receive a new title but no increase in responsibility; Employee Q would be placed in a position of increased responsibility. Consider the following statements about promotions and employee development:

The principle of unity of command states that each participant in a formal organisation should receive orders from and be responsible to only one superior. Fayol gave a lot of importance to this principle. He felt that if this principle is violated “authority is undermined, discipline is in jeopardy, order disturbed and stability threatened”. The principle resembles military organisation. Dual subordination should be avoided. This is to prevent confusion regarding tasks to be done. original_question.stem:
A delivery service sets a standard average delivery time of 20 minutes per delivery. During one shift, 10 completed deliveries took 180 minutes in total. Treat actual performance as the mean time per delivery.

(A) The mean actual time was 18 minutes per delivery.
(B) The total actual time of 180 minutes can be compared directly with 20 minutes per delivery because both use minutes.
(C) Before comparison, actual performance should be expressed as 18 minutes per delivery.
(D) The comparison should be made in deliveries per shift rather than time per delivery.

Which statements are correct? Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

records.original_explanation: The mean actual time is 180 ÷ 10 = 18 minutes per delivery, so (A) is correct. Expressing actual performance as 18 minutes per delivery gives it the same unit as the standard, so (C) is correct. (B) compares total time for 10 deliveries with time per delivery, while (D) changes the measure from time to deliveries.

reasons: failed:source_support
failed:source_support
The mean actual time is 180 ÷ 10 = 18 minutes per delivery, so statements A and C are true.

Statement B compares a total time with a per-delivery average; sharing the label “minutes” does not make those quantities comparable directly. Statement D changes the measure from time per delivery to deliveries per shift, contrary to the stated standard.
The source supports comparing actual performance with standards in the same units and in a manner that makes comparison easier.
source_support.syllabus_topic: Steps in the control process: measurement of actual performance and comparison with standards

answer_conditions.condition: The standard is 20 minutes per delivery.
Ten completed deliveries took 180 minutes in total.
Actual performance is to be treated as mean time per delivery.
The actual performance should be measured in the same units as the standard for comparison.
The resulting mean actual time is 18 minutes per delivery.

option_challenges.strongest_reading: Reading “same units” as minutes alone could make B seem true, but C still states the required mean actual performance, so A cannot be correct.
Treat the shift’s total time as comparable to the per-delivery standard and make shift throughput the comparison target.
If shift throughput rather than average delivery time were the target, deliveries per shift could be used; the stem specifies a time-per-delivery standard.

style_notes: The reference to one shift is incidental; the stated total, delivery count, and mean-performance instruction make the calculation determinate.

(iii) Unity of Command: This principle insists that a person in the organisation should receive instructions from one superior only. (iv) Appropriateness of direction tech­ nique: According to this principle, appropriate motivational and leadership technique should be used while directing the people based on subordinate needs, capabilities, attitudes and other situational variables. For example, for some people money can act as powerful motivator while for others promotion may act as effective motivator. (v) Managerial communication: Effe- ctive managerial communication across all the levels in the organisation makes direction effective. Directing should convey clear instructions to create total understanding to subordinates.

supporting_excerpts.text: The formal organisation can be better understood by a study of its features which are as follows: (a) It specifies the relationships among various job positions and the nature of their inter ­ relationship. This clarifies who has to report to whom. (b) It is a means to achieve the objectives specified in the plans, as it lays down rules and procedures essential for their achievement. (c) Efforts of various departments are coordinated, interlinked and integrated through the formal organisation. (d) It is deliberately designed by the top management to facilitate the smooth functioning of the organisation. (e) It places more emphasis on work to be performed than interpersonal relationships among the employees. Advantages: Formal organisation offers many advantages. Some of the important ones are: (a) It is easier to fix responsibility since mutual relationships are clearly defined. (b) There is no ambiguity in the role that each member has to play as duties are specified. This also helps in avoiding duplication of effort. (c) Unity of command is maintained through an established chain of command. (d) It leads to effective accomplish­ ment of goals by providing a framework for the operations to be performed and ensuring that each employee knows the r ole he has to play. (e) It provides stability to the organ­ isation. This is because behaviour of employees can be fairly pre­ dicted since there are specific rules to guide them.

Thus, a functional structure is an organisational design that groups similar or related jobs together. Advantages: The functional structure has many advantages to offer. Important among them are as follows: (a) A functional structure leads to occupational specialisation since emphasis is placed on specific functions. This pr omotes efficiency in utilisation of manpower as employees perform similar tasks within a department and are able to improve performance. (b) It promotes control and coordination within a department because of similarity in the tasks being perfor med. (c) It helps in increasing managerial and operational efficiency and this results in increased pr ofit. (d) It leads to minimal duplication of effort which results in economies of scale and this lowers cost. (e) It makes training of employees easier as the focus is only on a limited range of skills. (f) It ensures that different functions get due attention. Disadvantages: The functional structur e has certain disadvantages which an organisation must take into consideration before it adopts it. Some of them are as follows: (a) A functional structure places less emphasis on overall enterprise objectives than the objectives pursued by a functional head. Such practices may lead to functional empires wherein the importance of a particular function may be overemphasised. Pursuing departmental interests at the cost of organisational interests can also hinder the interaction between two or more departments. (b) It may lead to problems in coordination as information has to be exchanged across functionally differentiated departments.

original_question.stem:
For each case, calculate the signed deviation as actual performance minus the standard, after expressing both in the same unit. All actual results refer to the same period or basis as their standards. Use 60 seconds = 1 minute. For the defect-rate case, treat the observed rate as representative and scale it proportionally to 1,000 units.

Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) The weekly output standard is 1,200 pieces; actual output is 3 batches of 390 pieces each.
(B) The standard average customer waiting time is 8 minutes; the actual average is 510 seconds per customer.
(C) The standard is 6 defects per 1,000 pieces; actual production has 9 defects among 1,500 pieces.
(D) The weekly cost standard is ₹1,20,000; the actual weekly cost is ₹1,29,000.

List-II
(I) +₹9,000
(II) 0 defects per 1,000 pieces
(III) −30 pieces
(IV) +0.5 minute per customer

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

records.original_explanation: For (A), 3 × 390 = 1,170, giving 1,170 − 1,200 = −30 pieces; for (B), 510 seconds = 8.5 minutes, giving a deviation of +0.5 minute per customer. For (C), 9 defects among 1,500 pieces scales to 6 per 1,000, so the deviation is zero; for (D), ₹1,29,000 − ₹1,20,000 = +₹9,000. These matches compare actual performance with standards using the same units.

original_question.stem:
A firm is establishing a control procedure for one key result area. The manager must set up the procedure and then handle a deviation that qualifies for managerial attention. Arrange the following stages from earliest to latest:
(A) Set the critical point and permissible limit for the key result area.
(B) Identify a deviation that requires managerial attention by assessing it against the permissible limit.
(C) Bring the significant deviation beyond the permissible limit to management’s notice.
(D) Analyse the causes of the deviation requiring managerial attention.
Choose the correct sequence from the options given below:

records.original_explanation: The manager first establishes the critical point and permissible limit, then identifies which deviation requires attention. A deviation beyond that limit is brought to management’s notice, and the identified deviation is then analysed for its causes. The other sequences place identification before setting the limit, notification before confirming the deviation qualifies, or cause analysis before notification.

reasons: failed:source_support
failed:source_support

The excerpts support setting critical points and permissible limits, identifying significant deviations, bringing deviations beyond the permissible limit to management’s notice, and analysing causes after identifying deviations requiring attention. This supports the intended sequence A-B-C-D.

The excerpts do not clearly require notification to precede cause analysis. A manager could reasonably analyse the cause before escalating the deviation, making option D defensible under the printed stem.

original_question.stem:
A person who obtains goods or avails services for resale or commercial purpose is not treated as a consumer and is outside the scope of consumer protection. Match each case in List-I with the classification in List-II. For (C) and (D), neither resale nor commercial purpose applies; the classification must not imply any other eligibility.
List-I
(A) A shopkeeper obtains goods solely to resell them.
(B) A company avails a service solely for its commercial operations.
(C) A household obtains goods solely for household use, not for resale or commercial purpose.
(D) An individual avails a service solely for personal use, not for resale or commercial purpose.
List-II
(I) Goods obtained for resale; the stated purpose falls within the exclusion.
(II) Services availed for commercial purpose; the stated purpose falls within the exclusion.
(III) Goods obtained for neither resale nor commercial purpose; the stated purpose does not fall within this exclusion.
(IV) Services availed for neither resale nor commercial purpose; the stated purpose does not fall within this exclusion.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
A. (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
B. (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
C. (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
D. (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)

records.original_explanation: Goods obtained for resale and services availed for commercial purpose fall within the stated exclusion. The household goods and personal service in (C) and (D) are expressly not for resale or commercial purpose, so those stated uses do not fall within this exclusion. This matching classifies only the stated purpose and does not establish any other eligibility.

original_question.stem:
Two firms sell the same physical refrigerator model. Firm P also provides after-sales service, handles complaints and makes spare parts available; Firm Q offers none of these. Assume these are the only differences in their offers. Consider the following statements:
(A) The firms’ product offers are necessarily identical because their physical refrigerators are identical.
(B) Firm P’s after-sales service, complaint handling and spare-part availability may form part of the extended product.
(C) The firms’ total product offers may differ even though their physical refrigerators are identical.
(D) Support provided after purchase is outside the concept of product.
Which statements are correct?

records.original_explanation: The concept of product includes more than the physical item: it can include benefits to customers and an extended product, such as after-sales service, complaint handling and spare-part availability. Therefore, Firm P’s support may make its total product offer different from Firm Q’s, even though the physical refrigerators are identical. Statements (A) and (D) incorrectly exclude these aspects from the product concept.

reasons: failed:source_support
failed:source_support
The excerpts define product broadly to include benefits and the extended product, including after-sales services, complaint handling, and spare-part availability.

Thus B is correct and D is false. Since P and Q differ in the support they offer, their total product offers may differ despite identical refrigerators: C is correct and A is false. The correct combination is B and C (option D).

Financial Planning Financial planning is essentially the preparation of a financial blueprint of an organisation’s future operations. The objective of financial planning is to ensure that enough funds are available at right time. If adequate funds are not available the firm will not be able to honour its commitments and carry out its plans. On the other hand, if excess funds are available, it will unnecessarily add to the cost and may encourage wasteful expenditure. It must be kept in mind that financial planning is not equivalent to, or a substitute for, financial management. Financial management aims at choosing the best investment and financing alternatives by focusing on their costs and benefits. Its objective is to increase the shareholders’ wealth. Financial planning on the other hand aims at smooth operations by focusing on fund requirements and their availability in the light of financial decisions. For example, if a capital budgeting decisions is taken, the operations are likely to be at a higher scale. The amount of expenses and revenues are likely to increase. Financial planning process tries to forecast all the items which are likely to undergo changes. It enables the management to foresee the fund requirements both the quantum as well as the timing. Likely shortage and surpluses are forecast so that necessary activities are taken in advance to meet those situations. Thus, financial planning strives to achieve the following twin objectives. (a) To ensure availability of funds whenever requir ed: This include a proper estimation of the funds required for different purposes such as for the purchase of long- term assets or to meet day-to- day expenses of business etc. Apart from this, there is a need to estimate the time at which these funds are to be made available. Financial planning also tries to specify possible sources of these funds. (b) To see tha t the firm does not raise resources unnecessarily: Excess funding is almost as bad as inadequate funding. Even if there is some surplus money, good financial planning would put it to the best possible use so that the financial resources are not left idle and don’t unnecessarily add to the cost. Thus, a proper matching of funds requirements and their availability is sought to be achieved by financial planning. Thus, a functional structure is an organisational design that groups similar or related jobs together. Advantages: The functional structure has many advantages to offer. Important among them are as follows: (a) A functional structure leads to occupational specialisation since emphasis is placed on specific functions. This pr omotes efficiency in utilisation of manpower as employees perform similar tasks within a department and are able to improve performance. (b) It promotes control and coordination within a department because of similarity in the tasks being perfor med. (c) It helps in increasing managerial and operational efficiency and this results in increased pr ofit. (d) It leads to minimal duplication of effort which results in economies of scale and this lowers cost. (e) It makes training of employees easier as the focus is only on a limited range of skills. (f) It ensures that different functions get due attention. Disadvantages: The functional structur e has certain disadvantages which an organisation must take into consideration before it adopts it. Some of them are as follows: (a) A functional structure places less emphasis on overall enterprise objectives than the objectives pursued by a functional head. Such practices may lead to functional empires wherein the importance of a particular function may be overemphasised. Pursuing departmental interests at the cost of organisational interests can also hinder the interaction between two or more departments. (b) It may lead to problems in coordination as information has to be exchanged across functionally differentiated departments.

supporting_excerpts.text: Financial ManageMents 225 BUsiness st UDies 224 certain restrictions on the payment of dividends in future. The companies are required to ensure that the dividend does not violate the terms of the loan agreement in this regard. Financial Planning Financial planning is essentially the preparation of a financial blueprint of an organisation’s future operations. The objective of financial planning is to ensure that enough funds are available at right time. If adequate funds are not available the firm will not be able to honour its commitments and carry out its plans. On the other hand, if excess funds are available, it will unnecessarily add to the cost and may encourage wasteful expenditure. It must be kept in mind that financial planning is not equivalent to, or a substitute for, financial management. Financial management aims at choosing the best investment and financing alternatives by focusing on their costs and benefits. Its objective is to increase the shareholders’ wealth. Financial planning on the other hand aims at smooth operations by focusing on fund requirements and their availability in the light of financial decisions. For example, if a capital budgeting decisions is taken, the operations are likely to be at a higher scale. The amount of expenses and revenues are likely to increase. Financial planning process tries to forecast all the items which are likely to undergo changes. It enables the management to foresee the fund requirements both the quantum as well as the timing. Likely shortage and surpluses are forecast so that necessary activities are taken in advance to meet those situations. Thus, financial planning strives to achieve the following twin objectives. (a) To ensure availability of funds whenever requir ed: This include a proper estimation of the funds required for different purposes such as for the purchase of long- term assets or to meet day-to- day expenses of business etc. Apart from this, there is a need to estimate the time at which these funds are to be made available. Financial planning also tries to specify possible sources of these funds. (b) To see tha t the firm does not raise resources unnecessarily: Excess funding is almost as bad as inadequate funding. Even if there is some surplus money, good financial planning would put it to the best possible use so that the financial resources are not left idle and don’t unnecessarily add to the cost. Thus, a proper matching of funds requirements and their availability is sought to be achieved by financial planning. Consider the following facts: After forty years of planned development, India achieved a strong industrial base and became self-sufficient in the production of food grains. In 1991, a crisis in the balance of payments led to the introduction of economic reforms.

List-I
(A) Forty years of planned development
(B) Strong industrial base
(C) Self-sufficiency in the production of food grains
(D) 1991 balance-of-payments crisis

List-II
(I) Led to the introduction of economic reforms
(II) Achievement stated for India after planned development
(III) Achievement in food-grain production stated for India
(IV) Period after which the two achievements in (II) and (III) are reported

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
A. (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
B. (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
C. (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
D. (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)

Arrange the following steps in the correct sequence for constructing a market supply curve from the supply schedules of the same firms at a range of market prices.
(A) Add the quantities supplied by all firms at a given market price.
(B) Read the quantity supplied by each firm at that market price.
(C) Repeat the process for other market prices.
(D) Plot the aggregate quantity supplied against the corresponding market price.

supporting_excerpts.text: 67 under Perfect Competition The Theory of the Firm • In a perfectly competitive market, firms are price-takers. • The total revenue of a firm is the market price of the good multiplied by the firm’s output of the good. • For a price-taking firm, average revenue is equal to market price. • For a price-taking firm, marginal revenue is equal to market price. • The demand curve that a firm faces in a perfectly competitive market is perfectly elastic; it is a horizontal straight line at the market price. • The profit of a firm is the difference between total revenue earned and total cost incurred. • If there is a positive level of output at which a firm’s profit is maximised in the short run, three conditions must hold at that output level (i) p = SMC (ii) SMC is non-decreasing (iii) p ≥ AV C. • If there is a positive level of output at which a firm’s profit is maximised in the long run, three conditions must hold at that output level (i) p = LRMC (ii) LRMC is non-decreasing (iii) p ≥ LRAC. • The short run supply curve of a firm is the rising part of the SMC curve from and above minimum AVC together with 0 output for all prices less than the minimum AVC. • The long run supply curve of a firm is the rising part of the LRMC curve from and above minimum LRAC together with 0 output for all prices less than the minimum LRAC. • Technological progress is expected to shift the supply curve of a firm to the right. • An increase (decrease) in input prices is expected to shift the supply curve of a firm to the left (right). • The imposition of a unit tax shifts the supply curve of a firm to the left. • The market supply curve is obtained by the horizontal summation of the supply curves of individual firms. • The price elasticity of supply of a good is the percentage change in quantity supplied due to one per cent change in the market price of the good. ssssseeeeesssssiiiiicccccrrrrreeeeexxxxxEEEEE yyyyyrrrrraaaaammmmmmmmmmuuuuuSSSSS 1. original_question.stem: A planning review summarises two findings for India after forty years of planned development: (i) a strong industrial base had been achieved and food-grain production had become self-sufficient; (ii) a major segment of the population continued to depend on agriculture for its livelihood. Treat both findings as accurate. A reviewer argues that finding (ii) cannot be true once finding (i) is true. Which assessment best applies the findings?
options: The reviewer is correct: food-grain self-sufficiency rules out continued dependence on agriculture for livelihood.
The reviewer is correct: a strong industrial base rules out continued dependence on agriculture for livelihood.
The reviewer is incorrect: food-grain self-sufficiency can coexist with continued dependence on agriculture for livelihood.
The reviewer is incorrect: the food-grain achievement shows that the major segment dependent on agriculture had shifted to industrial livelihoods.

records.original_explanation: The findings concern food-grain production and livelihood dependence, respectively. The stated excerpt reports both outcomes together, so food-grain self-sufficiency does not rule out continued dependence on agriculture for livelihood.

original_question.stem:
Consider the following statements about the paradox of thrift. It states that if all people increase the proportion of income they save, total savings will not increase; they will either decline or remain unchanged. In an illustration, aggregate saving is 10 both before and after an increase in thrift.
(A) An increase in the proportion of income saved necessarily raises total savings.
(B) When people become more thrifty, total savings may remain unchanged.
(C) Total savings must decline whenever people become more thrifty.
(D) In the illustration, aggregate saving is 10 at both points.
Choose the correct answer using the options below:

records.original_explanation: The paradox of thrift states that total savings do not increase when people raise the proportion of income they save; savings may remain unchanged. In the illustration, aggregate saving is 10 both before and after the increase in thrift. Therefore, statements (B) and (D) are correct.

This result is known as the Paradox of ThriftParadox of ThriftParadox of ThriftParadox of ThriftParadox of Thrift – which states that as people become more thrifty they end up saving less or same as before. This result, though sounds apparently impossible, is actually a simple application of the model we have learnt. Let us continue with the example. Suppose at the initial equilibrium of Y = 250, there is an exogenous or autonomous shift in peoples’ expenditure pattern – they suddenly become more thrifty. This may happen due to a new information regarding an imminent war or some other impending disaster , which makes people mor e cir cumspect and conservative about their expenditures. Hence the mps of the economy increases, or , alter natively, the mpc decr eases fr om 0.8 to 0.5. At the initial income level of AD* 1 = Y * 1 = 250, this sudden decline in mpc will imply a decrease in aggregate consumption spending and hence in aggregate demand, AD = A + cY , by an amount equal to (0.8 – 0.5) 250 = 75. This can be regarded as an autonomous reduction in consumption expenditure, to the extent that the change in mpc is occurring from some exogenous cause and is not a consequence of changes in the variables of the model. But as aggregate demand decreases by 75, it falls short of the output Y * 1 = 250 and there emerges an excess supply equal to 75 in the economy. Stocks are piling up in warehouses and producers decide to cut the value of production by 75 in the next round to restore equilibrium in the market. But that would mean a reduction in factor payments in the next round and hence a reduction in income by 75. As income decreases people reduce consumption proportionately but, this time, according to the new value of mpc which is 0.5. Consumption expenditure, and hence aggregate demand, decreases by (0.5)75, which creates again an excess supply in the market. In the next round, therefore, producers reduce output further by (0.5)75. Income of the people decreases accordingly and consumption expenditure and aggregate demand goes down again by (0.5) 2 75. The process goes on. However, as can be inferr ed fr om the dwindling values of the successive round effects, the process is convergent. What is the total decrease in the value of output and aggregate demand? Add up the infinite series 75 + (0.5) 75 + (0.5) 2 75 + ........ ¥ and the total reduction in output turns out to be 75 1 – 0.5 = 150 But that means the new equilibrium output of the economy is only Y * 2 = 100. People are now saving S * 2 = Y * 2 – C * 2 = Y * 2 – ( C + c2.Y * 2 ) = 100 – (40 + 0.5 × 100) = 10 in aggregate, whereas under the previous equilibrium they were saving S * 1 = Y * 1 – C * 1 = Y * 1 – ( C + c1.Y * 1) = 250 – (40 + 0.8 × 250) = 10 at the previous mpc, c1 = 0.8. Total value of savings in the economy has, therefore, remained unchanged. When A changes the line shifts upwards or downwards in parallel. When c changes, however , the line swings up or down. original_question.stem:
An economy records the following changes:
Year 1 to Year 2: GDP index rises from 200 to 220; employed persons increase from 80 million to 84 million.
Year 2 to Year 3: GDP index rises from 220 to 242; employed persons remain at 84 million.
Calculate percentage changes using (final value − initial value) ÷ initial value × 100. For this question, an increase in the GDP index represents an increase in production of goods and services, and jobless growth means an increase in production without generating employment. Which statement is correct?
options: GDP grew by 10% in each interval; employment grew by 5% and then 0%, so Year 2 to Year 3 shows jobless growth.
GDP grew by 10% in each interval; employment grew by 5% in each interval, so neither interval shows jobless growth.
GDP grew by 10% in each interval; employment grew by 5% and then 0%, so Year 1 to Year 2 shows jobless growth.
GDP grew by 10% and 9.09% in the two intervals; employment grew by 5% and then 0%, so Year 2 to Year 3 shows jobless growth.

records.original_explanation: From Year 1 to Year 2, GDP growth is (220 − 200) ÷ 200 × 100 = 10%, and employment growth is (84 − 80) ÷ 80 × 100 = 5%. From Year 2 to Year 3, GDP growth is (242 − 220) ÷ 220 × 100 = 10%, while employment growth is 0%. Thus, production increases without generating employment in the second interval, which meets the stated meaning of jobless growth.

original_question.stem:
A review considers four issues in organic farming. Match each issue in List-I with the corresponding implication in List-II.

List-I
(A) Comparing organic yields with yields from modern agricultural farming during the initial years
(B) A small or marginal farmer considering adaptation to large-scale organic production
(C) Comparing organic produce with sprayed produce for blemishes and shelf life
(D) Planning the range of off-season crops under organic farming

List-II
(I) The choice of off-season crops is quite limited.
(II) Organic produce may have more blemishes and a shorter shelf life.
(III) Organic yields are lower during the initial years than yields from modern agricultural farming.
(IV) Small and marginal farmers may find adaptation to large-scale production difficult.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

A. (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
B. (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
C. (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
D. (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)

records.original_explanation: The initial-years yield comparison maps (A) to (III), and the scale-adaptation concern for small and marginal farmers maps (B) to (IV). The comparison with sprayed produce maps (C) to (II), while the limited choice of off-season crops maps (D) to (I). Therefore, option A gives the complete match.

original_question.stem: An account cites villagers’ use of e-mail as an example of transformation, projects e-governance as a way of the future, and states that the value of IT depends greatly on the existing level of economic development. It raises, without answering, whether IT-based services in rural areas lead to human development. An agency compares two rural areas with different existing levels of economic development. Which conclusion is supported by the stated principle?
options: The value of IT should be assessed in relation to each area’s existing level of economic development.
Villagers’ use of e-mail establishes that IT has equal value across the two areas.
The projection of e-governance establishes that IT’s value is independent of economic development.
The discussion question establishes that rural IT services lead to human development.

records.original_explanation: The stated relationship makes each area’s existing level of economic development relevant when assessing the value of IT. The e-mail example, the projection of e-governance and the open discussion question do not establish the conclusions in options B, C and D.

reasons: failed:syllabus_mapping
failed:syllabus_mapping
The cited principle says IT’s value depends greatly on the existing level of economic development, so assessing it in relation to each area’s level is supported.
The e-mail example and e-governance projection do not establish equal or development-independent value; the discussion question is expressly left unanswered.

But this will not make any difference to the basic result, because after paying wages the remainder of value added by a firm will be distributed between rent, interest and profits (together called operating surplus). Table 2.3: Distributions of factor incomes of firms A and B Firm A Firm B Wages 20 60 Profits 30 90 Recall that GDP by income method = sum total of factor incomes, which is equal to total wages received (workers of A and B) and total profits earned (by A and B), which is equal4 to 80 + 120 = 200. 2.2.4 Factor Cost, Basic Prices and Market Prices In India, the most highlighted measure of national income has been the GDP at factor cost. The Central Statistics Office (CSO) of the Government of India has been reporting the GDP at factor cost and at market prices. In its revision in January 2015 the CSO replaced GDP at factor cost with the GVA at basic prices, and the GDP at market prices, which is now called only GDP, is now the most highlighted measure. The idea of GVA has already been discussed: it is the value of total output produced in the economy less the value of intermediate consumption (the output which is used in production of output further, and not used in final consumption). Here we discuss the concept of basic prices. The distinction between factor cost, basic prices and market prices is based on the distinction between net production taxes (production taxes less production subsidies) and net product taxes (product taxes less product subsidies). Production taxes and subsidies are paid or received in relation to production and are independent of the volume of production such as land revenues, stamp and registration fee. Product taxes and subsidies, on the other hand, are paid or received per unit or product, e.g., excise tax, service tax, export and import duties etc. Factor cost includes only the payment to factors of production, it does not include any tax. In order to arrive at the market prices, we have to add to the factor cost the total indirect taxes less total subsidies. The basic prices lie in between: they include the production taxes (less production subsidies) but not product taxes (less product subsidies). Therefore in order to arrive at market prices we have to add product taxes (less product subsidies) to the basic prices. As stated above, now the CSO releases GVA at basic prices. Thus, it includes the net production taxes but not net product taxes. In order to arrive at the GDP (at market prices) we need to add net pr oduct taxes to GV A at basic prices. Thus, GVA at factor costs + Net production taxes = GVA at basic prices GVA at basic prices + Net product taxes = GVA at market prices Table 2.5 at the end of the chapter gives the figures for GDP (at market prices) and GVA at basic prices, while T able 2.6 gives the composition of GDP fr om expenditure side. original_question.stem:
The listed real per capita income values are ₹7,651 in 1951, ₹12,174 in 1981, ₹15,748 in 1991, ₹23,095 in 2001 and ₹94,054 in 2018–22. For each interval, calculate the increase by subtracting the earlier listed value from the later one; do not annualise the 2001–2018–22 difference.

(A) The increase from 1991 to 2001 was ₹7,347.
(B) The increase from 1981 to 1991 was ₹4,523.
(C) The increase from 2001 to 2018–22 was ₹70,959.

original_question.stem:
A producer plans to add ₹1,20,000 to inventory by the end of the year. To meet extra demand, she later sells goods worth ₹35,000 from that inventory. Assume no other changes to inventory occur. (A) The producer plans an addition of ₹1,20,000 to inventory.
(B) The producer sells ₹35,000 worth of goods from inventory to meet extra demand.
(C) The net increase in inventory is calculated as ₹1,20,000 − ₹35,000 = ₹85,000.
(D) The amount of ₹85,000 is identified as actual (ex post) investment.
Choose the correct sequence:
A. (A)-(C)-(B)-(D)
B. (B)-(A)-(C)-(D)
C. (A)-(B)-(C)-(D)
D. (A)-(B)-(D)-(C)

options: The conclusion follows because the 11.6-percentage-point rise in industry’s GDP share measures an equivalent movement of workers out of agriculture.

original_question.stem:
Arrange the statements in the logical order of the concluding argument, with the government response at the end.
(A) The structure of the workforce in India has changed.
(B) Newly emerging jobs are found mostly in the service sector.

supporting_excerpts.text: 4 INDIAN ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT 1.1 I NTRODUCTION The primary objective of this book, Indian Economic Development , is to familiarise you with the basic features of the Indian economy, and its development, as it is today, in the aftermath of Independence. However, it is equally important to know something about the country’s economic past even as you learn about its present state and future prospects. So, let us first look at the state of India’s economy prior to the country’s independence and form an idea of the various considerations that shaped India’ s post-independence development strategy. The structure of India’s present- day economy is not just of current making; it has its roots steeped in history, particularly in the period when India was under British rule which lasted for almost two centuries before India finally won its independence on 15 August 1947. The sole purpose of the British colonial rule in India was to reduce the country to being a raw material supplier for Great Britain’s own rapidly expanding modern industrial base. An understanding of the exploitative nature of this relationship is essential for any assessment of the kind and level of development which the Indian economy has been able to attain over the last seven and half decades. 1.2 1.2 LOW LEVEL OF ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT UNDER THE COLONIAL RULE India had an independent economy before the advent of the British rule. Though agriculture was the main source of livelihood for most people, yet, the country’s economy was characterised by various kinds of manufacturing activities. India was particularly well known for its handicraft industries in the fields of cotton and silk textiles, metal and precious stone works etc. These products enjoyed a worldwide market based on the reputation of the fine quality of material used and the high standards of craftsmanship seen in all imports from India (See Box 1.1). “India is the pivot of our Empire... If the Empire loses any other part of its Dominion we can survive, but if we lose India, the sun of our Empire will have set.” Victor Alexander Vruce, the Viceroy of British India in 1894 Box 1.1: Textile Industry in Bengal Muslin is a type of cotton textile which had its origin in Bengal, particularly, places in and around Dhaka (spelled during the pre-independence period as Dacca), now the capital city of Bangladesh. ‘Daccai Muslin’ had gained worldwide fame as an exquisite type of cotton textile. The finest variety of muslin was called malmal. Sometimes, foreign travellers also used to refer to it as malmal shahi or malmal khas implying that it was wor n by, or fit for , the royalty. Reprint 2026-27

The economic policies pursued by the colonial government in India were concerned more with the protection and promotion of the economic interests of their home country than with the development of the Indian economy. Such policies brought about a fundamental change in the structure of the Indian economy — transforming the country into supplier of raw materials and consumer of finished industrial products from Britain.

original_question.stem: A research team wants to investigate the economy as a whole, rather than the behaviour of an individual consumer or producer or the price and quantity in a single-commodity market. Which research question best fits this aim?
options: How are price and quantity determined in the market for one commodity?
How does an individual consumer behave in relation to one commodity?
How does total output in the economy grow over time?
How does an individual producer behave in producing one commodity?

records.original_explanation: The question about how total output in the economy grows over time concerns an aggregate measure and its change over time, so it is macroeconomic. The other questions concern a single-commodity market or an individual consumer or producer, which are microeconomic topics.

In macroeconomics, on the other hand, we try to get an understanding of the economy as a whole by focusing our attention on aggregate measures such as total output, employment and aggregate price level. Here, we are interested in finding out how the levels of these aggregate measures are determined and how the levels of these aggregate measures change over time. Some of the important questions that are studied in macroeconomics are as follows: What is the level of total output in the

economy? How is the total output determined? How does the total output grow over time? Are the resources of the economy (eg labour) fully employed? What are the reasons behind the unemployment of resources? Why do prices rise? original_question.stem: For one financial year, a government has a fiscal deficit of ₹8,40,000. Its interest payments are ₹1,20,000, and its interest receipts on net domestic lending are ₹20,000. Assume these are the only interest payments and receipts relevant to the calculation. What is the government’s primary deficit?

records.original_explanation: Net interest liabilities = ₹1,20,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹1,00,000. Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − net interest liabilities = ₹8,40,000 − ₹1,00,000 = ₹7,40,000, so option C is correct.

reasons: blind_key_contradiction
blind_key_contradiction
The supplied definition gives primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments: ₹8,40,000 − ₹1,20,000 = ₹7,20,000 (A).

The excerpt separately describes gross primary deficit using net interest liabilities; subtracting the ₹1,00,000 net interest liabilities gives ₹7,40,000, but that is not the measure named in the question.
source_support.syllabus_topic: Government budget: measures of government deficit, including primary deficit

answer_conditions.condition: The requested measure is primary deficit, rather than gross primary deficit.
Fiscal deficit is ₹8,40,000 for the stated financial year.
Interest payments are ₹1,20,000 for that financial year.
Interest receipts on net domestic lending are ₹20,000.
No other relevant interest payments or receipts are to be included.
For primary deficit, subtract interest payments from fiscal deficit; the excerpt distinguishes this from gross primary deficit calculated using net interest liabilities.

option_challenges.strongest_reading: Add net interest liabilities to the fiscal deficit: ₹8,40,000 + (₹1,20,000 − ₹20,000) = ₹9,40,000.
Interpret the requested measure as gross primary deficit and subtract net interest liabilities: ₹8,40,000 − (₹1,20,000 − ₹20,000) = ₹7,40,000.
Subtract only the interest receipt from fiscal deficit: ₹8,40,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹8,20,000.

style_notes: The interest-receipt figure is extraneous to the stated primary-deficit calculation and may cue the separate gross-primary-deficit measure.

original_question.stem: A trade analyst reviews two records. Record P lists unprocessed cotton sent from India to an overseas buyer. Record Q lists Indian cotton and silk textiles, metalwork, and precious-stone work bought in several countries; the buyers cite the materials’ fine quality and the makers’ craftsmanship. For this case, treat P as raw input and Q as completed goods. Which interpretation best distinguishes Q from P?
options: Record Q represents an overseas market for raw Indian inputs, since cotton is one of its listed items.
Record Q represents an overseas market for Indian handicrafts, supported by material quality and craftsmanship.
Record Q represents an overseas market for finished British industrial goods, purchased by buyers in India.

original_question.stem:
A firm records the following three successive long-run production transitions. In each transition, all inputs increase by the same proportion. Input prices remain unchanged, and each listed cost is the cost of the input bundle used for that output.
Interval I: Output rises from 80 to 120 units; input-bundle cost rises from ₹2,00,000 to ₹2,80,000.
Interval II: Output rises from 120 to 180 units; input-bundle cost rises from ₹2,80,000 to ₹4,20,000.
Interval III: Output rises from 180 to 270 units; input-bundle cost rises from ₹4,20,000 to ₹6,51,000.
Which option correctly classifies the returns to scale in Intervals I, II and III, respectively?
options: Interval I: CRS; Interval II: IRS; Interval III: DRS.
Interval I: IRS; Interval II: CRS; Interval III: DRS.
Interval I: DRS; Interval II: CRS; Interval III: IRS.
Interval I: IRS; Interval II: DRS; Interval III: CRS.

records.original_explanation: Output rises by 50% in each interval. With unchanged input prices and all inputs scaled by the same proportion, the input-bundle cost changes by the same proportion as the inputs. In Interval I, cost rises by 40%, less than output, so IRS operates; in Interval II, both rise by 50%, so CRS operates; in Interval III, cost rises by 55%, more than output, so DRS operates.

Shapes of the Long Run Cost Curves We have previously discussed the returns to scales. Now let us see their implications for the shape of LRAC. IRS implies that if we increase all the inputs by a certain proportion, output increases by more than that proportion. In other words, to increase output by a certain proportion, inputs need to be increased by less than that proportion. With the input prices given, cost also increases by a lesser proportion. For example, suppose we want to double the output. To do that, inputs need to be increased, but less than double. The cost that the firm incurs to hire those inputs therefore also need to be increased by less than double. What is happening to the average cost here? It must be the case that as long as IRS operates, average cost falls as the firm increases output. DRS implies that if we want to increase the output by a certain proportion, inputs need to be increased by more than that proportion. As a result, cost also increases by more than that proportion. So, as long as DRS operates, the average cost must be rising as the firm increases output. CRS implies a proportional increase in inputs resulting in a proportional increase in output. So the average cost remains constant as long as CRS operates. It is argued that in a typical firm IRS is observed at the initial level of production. This is then followed by the CRS and then by the DRS. Accordingly, the LRAC curve is a ‘U’-shaped curve. Its downward sloping part corresponds to IRS and upward rising part corresponds to DRS. At the minimum point of the LRAC curve, CRS is observed. Let us check how the LRMC curve looks like. For the first unit of output, both LRMC and LRAC are the same. Then, as output increases, LRAC initially falls, and then, after a certain point, it rises. As long as average cost is falling, marginal cost must be less than the average cost.

15 units, because average variable cost is at its minimum there.
20 units, because it is the largest feasible output.

original_question.stem:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Household use of wood, dung cake or other biomass as fuel
(B) LPG used as a household fuel
(C) Material fed into a gobar gas plant
(D) Material left after gas production

List-II
(I) Cattle dung
(II) A clean fuel that reduces household pollution to a large extent and minimises wastage
(III) Slurry that is a good organic fertiliser and soil conditioner
(IV) A practice associated with deforestation, reduction in green cover and air pollution

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

records.original_explanation: The use of wood, dung cake or other biomass as household fuel is linked to deforestation, reduced green cover and air pollution, while LPG reduces household pollution and minimises wastage. Cattle dung is fed into a gobar gas plant, and the slurry left over is a good organic fertiliser and soil conditioner; therefore, the correct mapping is (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(I), (D)-(III).

These terms, however, can be used with a different connotation. Consumption may denote not what people have actually consumed in a given year, but what they Reprint 2026-27
54 5454 5454Introductory Macroeconomics had planned to consume during the same period. Similarly, investment can mean the amount a producer plans to add to her inventory. It may be different from what she ends up doing. Suppose the producer plans to add Rs 100 worth goods to her stock by the end of the year. Her planned investment is, therefore, Rs 100 in that year. However, due to an unforeseen upsurge of demand for her goods in the market the volume of her sales exceeds what she had planned to sell and, to meet this extra demand, she has to sell goods worth Rs 30 from her stock. Therefore, at the end of the year , her inventory goes up by Rs (100 – 30) = Rs 70 only. Her planned investment is Rs 100 whereas her actual, or ex post, investment is Rs 70 only. We call the planned values of the variables – consumption, investment or output of final goods – their ex ante measures.

original_question.stem: A village committee reviews a proposed paper mill that would use forest materials as industrial raw material. The mill is projected to employ 600 workers, and 1,200 residents use the same forest to meet daily needs. The government has allocated the forestland, but the proposal does not assess whether industrial use would restrict residents’ access; employment is its only quantified benefit. The industrialist argues that the job estimate and the allocation establish that the proposal is acceptable. Which response is best supported?
options: Reject the proposal solely because it involves industrial use of forest materials.
Assess whether residents’ daily needs would be deprived and weigh that impact alongside the employment offered.
Approve the proposal because its projected jobs establish that its benefits exceed its costs.
Treat the forestland allocation as evidence that residents’ daily needs are protected.

records.original_explanation: The stated comparison makes the effect on people’s daily needs relevant when considering the employment offered by industrial use of forest materials. The proposal does not establish whether residents’ access would be restricted, so that impact must be assessed rather than treating the job estimate or land allocation as decisive.

reasons: failed:source_support

original_question.stem:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I
(A) Growth of aggregate real output during the first half of the twentieth century
(B) Growth of per capita output per year
(C) The colonial government’s attempt to estimate national and per capita income
(D) The estimator whose estimates during the colonial period were considered very significant
List-II
(I) V.K.R.V. Rao
(II) Less than 2 per cent
(III) No sincere attempt
(IV) Half per cent per year
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

records.original_explanation: Aggregate real output growth is matched with less than 2 per cent, while per capita output growth per year is matched with half per cent. The colonial government made no sincere attempt to estimate national and per capita income, and V.K.R.V. Rao’s estimates were considered very significant. These matches give option D.

reasons: failed:source_support
failed:source_support
The source states that aggregate real output grew by less than 2 per cent (II), while per capita output grew by half a per cent per year (IV).
It also states there was no sincere colonial-government attempt to estimate national and per capita income (III), and that V.K.R.V. Rao's estimates were considered very significant (I).
These matches give option D. No arithmetic is required; the percentages are matched to their stated measures.

original_question.stem:
In each case, the initially announced fixed exchange rate is ₹80 per unit of foreign currency. The quote is expressed in rupees per unit of foreign currency, and the change is made by the government. Calculate the percentage change relative to ₹80 and match each case with its interpretation.

List-I
(A) The government raises the quote from ₹80 to ₹88.
(B) The government lowers the quote from ₹80 to ₹72.
(C) The government raises the quote from ₹80 to ₹84.
(D) The government lowers the quote from ₹80 to ₹76.

List-II
(I) Increase of 10%; devaluation; domestic currency becomes cheaper
(II) Decrease of 10%; revaluation; domestic currency becomes costlier
(III) Increase of 5%; devaluation; domestic currency becomes cheaper
(IV) Decrease of 5%; revaluation; domestic currency becomes costlier

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

records.original_explanation: The changes from ₹80 are ₹8 for (A) and (B), or 10%, and ₹4 for (C) and (D), or 5%. An increase in the exchange rate in a fixed system is devaluation, which makes the domestic currency cheaper; a decrease is revaluation, which makes it costlier. Therefore, the matching in option A is correct.

supporting_excerpts.text: In a fixed exchange rate system, when some government action increases the exchange rate (thereby, making domestic currency cheaper) is called Devaluation. On the other hand, a Revaluation is said to occur, when the Government decreases the exchange rate (thereby, making domestic currency costlier) in a fixed exchange rate system.

86 86868686Introductory Macroeconomics economic agents will accept a national currency only if they are convinced that the amount of goods they can buy with a certain amount of that currency will not change frequently. In other words, the currency will maintain a stable purchasing power. Without this confidence, a currency will not be used as an international medium of exchange and unit of account since there is no international authority with the power to force the use of a particular currency in international transactions. In the past, governments have tried to gain confidence of potential users by announcing that the national currency will be freely convertible at a fixed price into another asset. Also, the issuing authority will have no control over the value of that asset into which the currency can be converted. This other asset most often has been gold, or other national currencies. There are two aspects of this commitment that has affected its credibility — the ability to convert freely in unlimited amounts and the price at which this conversion takes place. The international monetary system has been set up to handle these issues and ensure stability in international transactions. With the increase in the volume of transactions, gold ceased to be the asset into which national currencies could be converted (See Box 6.2). Although some national currencies have international acceptability, what is important in transactions between two countries is the currency in which the trade occurs. For instance, if an Indian wants to buy a good made in America, she would need dollars to complete the transaction. If the price of the good is ten dollars, she would need to know how much it would cost her in Indian rupees. That is, she will need to know the price of dollar in terms of rupees. The price of one currency in terms of another currency is known as the foreign exchange rate or simply the exchange rate . We will discuss this in detail in section 6.2. 6.1 THE BALANCE OF PAYMENTS The balance of payments (BoP) record the transactions in goods, services and assets between residents of a country with the rest of the world for a specified time period typically a year. There are two main accounts in the BoP — the current account and the capital account1. 6.1.1 Current Account Current Account is the record of trade in goods and services and transfer payments. Figure 6.1 illustrates the components of Current Account. Trade in goods includes exports and imports of goods. Trade in services includes factor income and non-factor income transactions. Transfer payments are the receipts which the residents of a country get for ‘free’, without having to provide any goods or services in return. They consist of gifts, remittances and grants. They could be given by the government or by private citizens living abroad. 1 There is a new classification in which the balance of payments have been divided into three accounts — the current account, the financial account and the capital account. This is as per the new accounting standards specified by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in the sixth edition of the Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual (BPM6). India has also made the change but the Reserve Bank of India continues to publish data accounting to the old classification. Reprint 2026-27

In the next period the firms will once again produce goods and services and pay remunerations to the factors of production. These remunerations will once again be used to buy the goods and services. Hence year after year we can imagine the aggregate income of the economy going through the two sectors, firms and households, in a circular way. This is represented in Fig. 2.1. When the income is being spent on the goods and services produced by the firms, it takes the form of aggregate expenditure received by the firms. Since the value of expenditure must be equal to the value of goods and services, we can equivalently measure the aggregate income by “calculating the aggregate value of goods and services pr oduced by the fir ms”. When the aggr egate revenue received by the firms is paid out to the factors of production it takes the form of aggregate income. In Fig. 2.1, the uppermost arrow, going from the households to the firms, represents the spending the households undertake to buy goods and services produced by the firms. The second arrow going from the firms to the households is the counterpart of the arrow above. It stands for the goods and services which are flowing from the firms to the households. In other words, this flow is what the households are getting from the firms, for which they are making the expenditures. In short, the two arrows on the top represent the goods and services market – the arrow above represents the flow of payments for the goods and services, the arrow below represents the flow of goods and services. The two arrows at the bottom of the diagram similarly represent the factors of production market. The lower most arrow going from the households to the firms symbolises the services that the households are rendering to the firms. Using these services the firms are manufacturing the output. The arrow above this, going from the firms to the households, represents the payments made by the firms to the households for the services provided by the latter. Since the same amount of money, representing the aggregate value of goods and services, is moving in a circular way, if we want to estimate the aggregate value of goods and services produced during a year we can measure the annual value of the flows at any of the dotted lines indicated in the diagram. W e can measure the uppermost flow (at point A) by measuring the aggregate value of spending that the firms receive for the final goods and services which they produce. original_question.stem:
A colonial official is reported as saying: “India is the pivot of our Empire... If the Empire loses any other part of its Dominion we can survive, but if we lose India, the sun of our Empire will have set.” The statement is attributed to Victor Alexander Vruce, Viceroy of British India in 1894. Match each part of the statement or its attribution in List-I with the interpretation it supports in List-II.

List-I
(A) The official says the Empire could survive the loss of any other part of its Dominion.
(B) The official says that if India were lost, the sun of the Empire would have set.
(C) The official describes India as the “pivot” of the Empire.
(D) The attribution identifies the speaker as Viceroy of British India in 1894.

List-II
(I) Identifies the speaker’s office and the year of the statement
(II) Presents India as central to the Empire
(III) Presents the loss of another dominion as survivable
(IV) Presents the loss of India as the end of the Empire

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

supporting_excerpts.text: 4 INDIAN ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT 1.1 I NTRODUCTION The primary objective of this book, Indian Economic Development , is to familiarise you with the basic features of the Indian economy, and its development, as it is today, in the aftermath of Independence. However, it is equally important to know something about the country’s economic past even as you learn about its present state and future prospects. So, let us first look at the state of India’s economy prior to the country’s independence and form an idea of the various considerations that shaped India’ s post-independence development strategy. The structure of India’s present- day economy is not just of current making; it has its roots steeped in history, particularly in the period when India was under British rule which lasted for almost two centuries before India finally won its independence on 15 August 1947. The sole purpose of the British colonial rule in India was to reduce the country to being a raw material supplier for Great Britain’s own rapidly expanding modern industrial base. An understanding of the exploitative nature of this relationship is essential for any assessment of the kind and level of development which the Indian economy has been able to attain over the last seven and half decades. 1.2 1.2 LOW LEVEL OF ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT UNDER THE COLONIAL RULE India had an independent economy before the advent of the British rule. Though agriculture was the main source of livelihood for most people, yet, the country’s economy was characterised by various kinds of manufacturing activities. India was particularly well known for its handicraft industries in the fields of cotton and silk textiles, metal and precious stone works etc. These products enjoyed a worldwide market based on the reputation of the fine quality of material used and the high standards of craftsmanship seen in all imports from India (See Box 1.1). “India is the pivot of our Empire... If the Empire loses any other part of its Dominion we can survive, but if we lose India, the sun of our Empire will have set.” Victor Alexander Vruce, the Viceroy of British India in 1894 Box 1.1: Textile Industry in Bengal Muslin is a type of cotton textile which had its origin in Bengal, particularly, places in and around Dhaka (spelled during the pre-independence period as Dacca), now the capital city of Bangladesh. ‘Daccai Muslin’ had gained worldwide fame as an exquisite type of cotton textile. The finest variety of muslin was called malmal. Sometimes, foreign travellers also used to refer to it as malmal shahi or malmal khas implying that it was wor n by, or fit for , the royalty. The economic policies pursued by the colonial government in India were concerned more with the protection and promotion of the economic interests of their home country than with the development of the Indian economy. Such policies brought about a fundamental change in the structure of the Indian economy — transforming the country into supplier of raw materials and consumer of finished industrial products from Britain.

original_question.stem:
A rural planning team is identifying water-body types relevant to a fishing community. The team is classifying types, not asserting that fishing takes place at each particular site. Consider the following statements.
(A) A local lake and stream may be included among the water bodies described as an integral, life-giving source.
(B) The description “mother” or “provider” reflects how the fishing community regards the water body.
(C) The water bodies relevant to this description are restricted to seas and oceans.
(D) Rivers and natural aquatic ponds are also among the water bodies named.
Choose the correct answer:

records.original_explanation: The listed water bodies include lakes, streams, rivers and natural aquatic ponds, and they are described as an integral, life-giving source for the fishing community. The community regards the water body as a “mother” or “provider”. Statement (C) is incorrect because the description is not restricted to seas and oceans.

Four developments concerning pesticide control are listed below.
1. Milk, meat and fish were found to be contaminated.
2. Efforts were made to bring in better methods of pest control.

4. Pest-controlling chemicals isolated from neem were being used.

supporting_excerpts.text: Similarly, in a flexible exchange rate regime, when the price of domestic currency (rupees) in terms of foreign currency (dollars) increases, it is called Appreciation of the domestic currency (rupees) in terms of foreign currency (dollars).

Fixed Exchange Rates In this exchange rate system, the Government fixes the exchange rate at a particular level. In Fig. 6.3, the market determined exchange rate is e. However, let us suppose that for some reason the Indian Government wants to encourage exports for which it needs to make rupee cheaper for foreigners it would do so by fixing a higher exchange rate, say Rs 70 per dollar from the current exchange rate of Rs 50 per dollar. Thus, the new exchange rate set by the Government is e1, where e1 > e. At this exchange rate, the supply of dollars exceeds the demand for dollars. The RBI intervenes to purchase the dollars for rupees in the foreign exchange market in order to absorb this excess supply which has been marked as AB in the figure. Thus, through intervention, the Government can maintain any exchange rate in the economy. But it will be accumulating more and more foreign exchange so long as this intervention goes on. On the other hand if the goverment was to set an exchange rate at a level such as e 2, there would be an excess demand for dollars in the foreign exchange market. To meet this excess demand for dollars, the government would have to withdraw dollars from its past holdings of dollars. If it fails to do so, a black market for dollars may come up. In a fixed exchange rate system, when some government action increases the exchange rate (thereby, making domestic currency cheaper) is called Devaluation. On the other hand, a Revaluation is said to occur, when the Government decreases the exchange rate (thereby, making domestic currency costlier) in a fixed exchange rate system.

metadata.topic: Match the Following: focus on this supplied section: no longer used because something new has been invented. Test a distinct implication, application or calculation supported by it.

original_question.stem:
Match each case in List-I with the appropriate assessment in List-II. Use only the information stated in each case.

List-I
(A) An old scanner is no longer used because a newly invented scanner has replaced it.
(B) A printer is no longer used because it broke; no new device replaced it.
(C) An older radio remains in regular use, although a newer radio has been invented.
(D) A new audio player has just been invented; no earlier player is said to have stopped being used because of it.

List-II
(I) Both the end of use and the new invention as its cause are stated.
(II) The item is still in use.
(III) The item is no longer used, but a new invention is not given as the cause.
(IV) A new invention is mentioned, but no earlier item is said to have stopped being used because of it.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

records.original_explanation: The definition requires that something is no longer used because something new has been invented. This condition is stated for (A); for (B), the stated reason is that the printer broke, while (C) remains in use and (D) gives no earlier item that stopped being used because of the invention.

reasons: failed:independent_evaluation
failed:independent_evaluation

B matches III, C matches II, and D matches IV. This gives option C.

(A) Volunteers then placed the chairs according to that completed list.
(B) When the arrangement was ready, the organiser checked it against the groups' replies.
(C) The organiser first asked each group how many chairs it needed.
(D) After collecting the replies, she prepared a seating list.
Choose the correct sequence from the options given below:

records.original_explanation: The organiser first asks each group for its chair requirement, then prepares a seating list after collecting the replies. The volunteers place the chairs according to that completed list, and the organiser checks the arrangement when it is ready. Therefore, the correct order is C-D-A-B.

reasons: failed:source_support

original_question.passage: Rain had washed the chalk game from the lane. The children arrived with fresh chalk and began drawing again. original_question.stem:
The following four sentences form a paragraph about one fictional class-project account. Arrange them in a coherent order.
(A) This qualification limits the claim to the particular project described.
(B) The account describes Tara’s actions in a fictional class project.
(C) It presents those actions in an explicit sequence.
(D) It does not prescribe that sequence as a universal method for preparing every display.
Choose the correct sequence from the options given below:

records.original_explanation: Sentence (B) introduces the account and its actions, which sentence (C) refers to as “those actions.” Sentence (D) qualifies the sequence introduced in (C), and “This qualification” in (A) refers to the limitation stated in (D).

original_question.stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
The clerk was ____ in carrying out her assigned audit duties: she carefully checked each entry and put effort into completing every required correction.

records.original_explanation: The sentence describes care and effort in carrying out assigned work, which is the stated sense of "diligent". reasons: failed:source_support
failed:source_support
“Diligent” is the strongest direct match: its supplied definition is care and effort in work or duties, both of which the sentence states.

However, “vigilant” is also defensible: in an audit context, carefully checking every entry can reasonably be read as watchfulness for errors or trouble. The sentence does not rule out that reading, so the item does not have a single defensible answer.
